tags.gist: Says for augmentative communication devices only the no-device comparator describes reality, since no clinician can supply the user's own expression.
Argues the no-device baseline is not a floor on performance: a fabricated utterance lands below zero because without the device no false record exists.
Explains that for nonverbal users the comparator is no intervention, under which a plausible wrong output is a categorical harm rather than partial success.
Reports measurements in which a transcriber produced fluent words, including a sixteen-word sentence, from audio windows carrying no live signal.
Shows that panel, standard-of-care and median-clinician comparators score a fabricated sentence as underperformance, while only the absence comparator records a manufactured fact.
Says the absence comparator measures benefit poorly and should not replace the others; it serves as a floor test for output worse than nothing.
Recommends the absence comparator alongside the Section V.C comparators as a pass-or-fail gate that good panel performance cannot offset.
Proposes three tests for requiring the absence comparator: no human performs the function, the user cannot contest output, and errors leave a durable attributed record.
Proposes a null-input test scoring any output from signal-free input as failure, and would read element S.3 to cover false confidence that input was received.
Clarifies the measurements came from a commercial assistant, offered since the failure class belongs to any sensor-plus-generative architecture.
Takes no position on justifying a comparator where a human alternative exists but is unavailable in practice.
Claims narrowly that where a device's function is the user's expression, omitting the absence comparator records fabricated utterances as partial credit.
Says only the comparator asks what the record would hold without the device; for nonverbal users that is nothing, sometimes the safer result.
